## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson desc-lesson"><p>Imagine that eleven students completed a hypothetical attention test. Is a single average enough to describe their scores? In this activity, we will explore how the shape of a distribution, unusual observations, and variability affect the statistics we use to summarize data.</p><p>This optional lesson supports Weeks 3–4 of the proposed Elementary Statistics course. All scores are illustrative, not actual student data.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Describe a distribution using dot plots and histograms, and explain how bin width affects a histogram.</li><li>Compare mean and median and explain their sensitivity to unusual observations.</li><li>Interpret sample standard deviation and compare distributions with the same mean but different variability.</li><li>Interpret a standardized score in relation to its reference distribution.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review quantitative variables, frequency, and the idea of an average.</p></div></div>
~~~

<div class="clt-lesson desc-lesson" id="desc-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>If the highest score moves from 62 to 95, which measure of center will change more?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-prediction" value="mean"> The mean.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-prediction" value="median"> The median.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-prediction" value="same"> Both will change by the same amount.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="desc-explore"><h2 id="desc-explore">1. Both samples have mean 50.</p><div class="clt-control"><label for="desc-factor">Sample B spread multiplier: <output data-output="factor">2.00×</output></label><input id="desc-factor" type="range" min="0.5" max="2.5" step="0.25" value="2" aria-describedby="desc-factor-help"><span class="clt-help" id="desc-factor-help">1× makes the samples identical. Values above 1 spread the scores farther from 50; values below 1 bring them closer.</span></div><div class="clt-action-row"><button class="clt-btn clt-secondary" type="button" data-action="reset-spread">Reset second activity</button></div><div class="desc-chart-wrap" data-chart="spread"></div><div class="desc-legend"><span><i class="desc-key mean" aria-hidden="true"></i>Mean and mean ± 1 SD span</span><span class="desc-reference">Dotted orange line: reference score 56</span></div><p class="clt-help" data-output="spread-description" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><table class="desc-table"><caption>Compare the two samples on the same score scale</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Statistic</th><th scope="col">Sample A</th><th scope="col">Sample B</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Mean</th><td data-output="meanA">—</td><td data-output="meanB">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Sample SD</th><td data-output="sdA">—</td><td data-output="sdB">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Range</th><td data-output="rangeA">—</td><td data-output="rangeB">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">z-score of reference 56</th><td data-output="zA">—</td><td data-output="zB">—</td></tr></tbody></table><details><summary>View the two sets of scores</summary><p>Sample A: <span data-output="scoresA"></span></p><p>Sample B: <span data-output="scoresB"></span></p></details><p class="clt-caption">The reference score of 56 is held fixed for comparison; it is not added to either dataset. A z-score expresses the distance from a reference mean in standard deviation units, not a probability or percentile by itself.</p></section></div>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson desc-lesson"><ol><li>Reset Activity 1 and change the selected score from 62 to 95. Record the mean, median, range and sample SD before and after. Which measures respond most? Why does the median stay fixed?</li><li>Choose the right-skewed, left-skewed and two-cluster datasets. Describe what you see in the dot plot and histogram. Compare the mean with the median. Do not use their ordering alone to diagnose skewness.</li><li>Keep the scores fixed and switch the bin width from 5 to 20. Does the shape look different? Do any numerical summaries change?</li><li>In Activity 2, compare multipliers of 0.5, 1 and 2. Why do the means stay equal? What happens to the standard deviation and the z-score of 56 as variability grows?</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> If two study conditions have the same average attention score, what else should a researcher report before comparing their outcomes?</p></div>
~~~

## What are the summaries telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson desc-lesson"><p>A <strong>distribution</strong> describes the values a variable takes and how frequently those values occur. A dot plot shows individual observations; a histogram groups quantitative observations into adjacent intervals. The binning changes the picture, not the underlying data.</p><p>The mean uses every value. The median depends on the middle position of ordered scores. An extreme observation can pull the mean toward it even when the median barely changes. The mode identifies the most frequent value(s), if there are repeats. No single summary fully describes a distribution.</p><div class="desc-formula"><strong>How we calculate variability</strong><br>Range = maximum − minimum<br>IQR = Q3 − Q1<br>Sample variance = sum of squared deviations from the sample mean / (n − 1)<br>Sample SD = square root of sample variance<br>Standardized score = (score − reference mean) / reference SD</div><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> Standard deviation measures how spread out scores are around the mean in the original score units. Squaring deviations gives larger deviations more influence. In Activity 2 we multiply every deviation from 50 by the same factor, so the mean stays 50 and the sample SD is multiplied by that factor. When spread increases, the same six-point difference is fewer SD units.</p><p>Use the sample mean and sample SD when describing these particular samples. Later, when working with a theoretical population, we use its population mean and population SD. A z-score describes relative location; a normal model or another distribution is needed to convert it into a probability. Outliers warrant investigation, not automatic deletion.</p></div>
~~~

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson desc-lesson" id="desc-knowledge-check"><p>These four questions revisit the learning goals. Which graph groups quantitative scores into contiguous intervals?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-shape" value="bar"> A bar chart for categories.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-shape" value="hist"> A histogram.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-shape" value="scatter"> A scatterplot of two variables.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="center"><legend>2. Which measure of center is generally more resistant to one very high observation?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-center" value="mean"> The mean.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-center" value="median"> The median.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-center" value="sd"> The standard deviation.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="spread"><legend>3. Two samples have mean 50. What can we conclude about their standard deviations?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-spread" value="same"> They must be equal.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-spread" value="zero"> They must both be zero.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-spread" value="different"> They may be different; the average alone does not establish spread.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="z"><legend>4. A score of 56 is six points above the mean of two samples. In the sample with the larger SD, how does its z-score compare?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-z" value="farther"> It is farther from zero.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-z" value="same"> It is exactly the same.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="desc-q-z" value="closer"> It is closer to zero.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> Look at the whole distribution. Report center and variability together, and interpret standardized scores relative to the distribution used.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapter 2 (descriptive statistics), and Section 6.1 (standardized scores in the normal distribution).</p></div>
